en: The Sūtra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Nanda and Jīvaka, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Rājagṛha with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus.
Accompanied by two hundred and fifty people, including bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and the eight classes of devas and nāgas, he gathered a great assembly to preach the Dharma.
At that time, the people of the world gave in measureless abundance.
There was a poor man who possessed only a single, worn-out hand-towel. Desiring to give it as an offering, he hesitated, fearing that the object was of poor quality and remaining undecided.
At that time, a bhikṣuṇī named Ambapālī was in the assembly; she rose from her seat, adjusted her robes, paid homage, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!...”
I recalled that in a previous life, I was born in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as a poor woman.
At that time, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa, who was then preaching the Dharma, surrounded by a great assembly.

Sitting there, he heard the sutra and was filled with joy; wishing to practice giving, he looked around but found nothing to offer. Reflecting on his own poverty and low status, his heart was moved by deep sorrow. He went to another’s orchard to beg for fruits and melons, intending to give them to the Buddha.
At that time, he obtained a single pomegranate, large and fragrant. Carrying a bowl of water along with the one fruit, he offered them to Kāśyapa Buddha and the assembly of monks.
Knowing his sincere devotion, the Buddha accepted them with a prayer of blessing and distributed the water and the fruit, reaching everyone everywhere.
By virtue of this merit, when her life ended, she was reborn in heaven and became a celestial queen;

later descending to the human world, she was not born from a womb, but was born within a mango flower for ninety-one kalpas, remaining upright and pure, always conscious of her past lives, until now she has encountered the World-Honored One, who has opened for her the eye of the Path.
At that time, the maiden Āmrapālī spoke in verse:
“The Three Honored Ones’ compassionate moisture is universal; In the perfection of wisdom, there is neither male nor female.
By giving fruit as an offering, one receives a vast reward; Through these conditions, one attains liberation from all suffering.”
"Born within the lotuses of this world, she shall become a Queen of Heaven;
having taken refuge in the protection of the Noble Assembly, she is the most profound and deep field of merit.
Having paid her respects, the Bhikṣuṇī Āmrapālī returned to her seat.

During the time when the Buddha was in the world, a mango tree grew spontaneously within the royal park of King Vijaya. Its branches and leaves were lush and abundant, and its fruit was exceptionally large; it possessed a radiant luster, and its fragrance and flavor were extraordinary.
The king cherished this mango so dearly that no one except the noble ladies of the inner palace was permitted to eat it.

In the kingdom there was a brahmin householder whose wealth was beyond counting and who was peerless in the land; moreover, he was intelligent, widely learned, and possessed extraordinary talent and wisdom. The king held him in high esteem and appointed him as his chief minister.
The king invited the brahmin to a meal; when the meal was finished, he gave him a mango fruit.
Seeing that the fragrance and flavor of the mango were extraordinary, the brahmin asked the king:
"Under this mango tree, might there be a small sapling that I might beg for?"
The king said:
"There are many small saplings; I feared they would obstruct the large trees, so I removed them.
If you wish to have them, I shall now give them to you."
He immediately gave a mango sapling to the brahmin.

Having received it, the brahmin returned home and planted it; he watered it morning and evening, and day by day it grew larger, its branches and twigs becoming lush and beautiful. After three years, it bore fruit, whose luster and size were like those of the royal family’s mangoes.
The brahmin was greatly delighted and thought to himself:
"My family's wealth is countless and no less than that of the king; it was only because I lacked this mango that I felt inferior. Now that I have obtained it, I am no different from the king."
He immediately took some to eat, but it was extremely bitter and astringent, such that he could not consume it at all.
The brahmin became even more distressed and anxious, and then withdrew to reflect:
"This must simply be because the soil here lacks fertility and moisture."
He then took the milk from a hundred cows and gave it to a single cow to drink; he then took the milk of that one cow and boiled it down into ghee, which he used to irrigate the mango root.
He watered it day after day until the following year, when its fruit became as sweet and delicious as the royal *nālikera* (coconut) tree.
Beside this *nālikera* tree, a gall-like growth suddenly appeared, as large as a clenched fist, growing larger day by day. The Brahmin thought to himself:
"Now that this gall has appeared, I fear it will damage the fruit."
Just as he was about to cut it away, he feared he might further injure the tree; he reflected upon this for many days, hesitating and unable to decide.
Then, from within the joint, a branch suddenly sprouted, pointing straight upward—tall, straight, and well-proportioned—rising above the treetop to a height of seventy feet from the ground.
At its tip, it branched out in various directions, spreading around like an inverted canopy; its flowers and leaves were so lush and beautiful that they surpassed those of the original tree.
The brahmin marveled at this, wondering, "I do not know what there might be upon these branches."
He then constructed a wooden gallery and ascended it to look out.
Within the canopy formed by the spreading branches, he saw a pool of water that was both clear and fragrant, and there were various flowers of brilliant and vivid colors.
Upon parting the flowers and looking beneath them, he found a young girl in the water of the pond; the Brahmin took her up, raised her, and named her Ambapālī.
When she reached the age of fifteen, her countenance was so upright and peerless that she was unmatched in all the world; her fame spread to distant lands.
Seven kings came simultaneously to the brahmin’s residence, seeking to marry the daughter of Nāda to serve as their queen.
The brahmin was greatly terrified, not knowing to whom he should give her.
He then constructed a high tower within his garden and placed the pomegranate maiden atop it. Coming forth, he addressed the kings, saying:
"This girl was not born of me; she emerged spontaneously from above a pomegranate tree. I do not know whether she is a daughter of a deva, a nāga, or a yakṣa."
"Is it a demonic entity?
Now that the seven kings seek it, if I were to give it to one king, the other six would surely be enraged; I dare not begrudge it to them.

The girl is currently on the upper terrace of the garden pavilion. Let the kings deliberate among themselves, and whichever one deems himself worthy shall take her away by his own means; this is not within my control."
Thereupon, the seven kings vied with one another for possession, their dispute remaining unresolved until the night fell.
At that time, King Bimbisāra entered through a secret subterranean passage, ascended the tower, and stayed there with him for the night.
As he was about to depart at dawn, the maiden Nāḍikā addressed him, saying:
"Great King! It was by your gracious majesty that you deigned to receive me; now you abandon me once more and depart."
"If she has a son, he will be of royal lineage; to whom should he be entrusted?
The king said, "If it is a boy, you must return him to me."
"If it is a daughter, I shall give her to you.
The king then removed the signet ring from his hand and gave it to the girl Nanda as a token of faith.
He then went out and addressed his ministers, saying:
"I have already obtained the maiden Nanda for one night; there is nothing extraordinary about it, so I am like an ordinary man, and thus I do not accept [the crown].
Within King Bimbisāra’s army, everyone cried out "Long live the King!
saying, "Our King has already obtained the maiden Nanda."
Upon hearing this, the six kings each returned to their own lands.
After King Bimbisāra had departed, the maiden Ambapālī subsequently became pregnant.
At that time, she commanded the gatekeeper, saying:
"If anyone should come seeking to see me, you must tell them that I am ill.
Later, when the moon was full, she gave birth to a son of handsome and upright countenance; as soon as the boy was born, he held a pouch of needles and medicine in his hand.
The brahmin said, "This is the son of the king, yet he holds medical instruments; he must surely be a physician-king.

At that time, the daughter of Nāla wrapped the child in white cloth and commanded a maidservant to carry him away and discard him in an alleyway. The maidservant, having received the command, took the child in her arms and went to abandon him there.
At that time, Prince Abhaya, mounting his carriage at dawn, went to see the Great King and dispatched men to clear and sweep the road.
Then, seeing a white object in the distance on the road, the prince stopped his carriage and asked those beside him,
"What is this white object?"
He replied, "This is a small child. He asked:
"Is he dead or alive?
He replied,
"He is still alive."
The prince ordered someone to take him up and immediately sought out a wet nurse to raise him to life.
The brahmin then took this young boy back and entrusted him to the daughter of Nāḍika, naming him Jīvaka.

By the time he was eight years old, he possessed brilliant intelligence and exceptional talent; his learning and calligraphy far surpassed those of his peers. When playing with the young children of his neighborhood, his mind was always disdainful of them, considering them inferior to himself.
The children all reviled him together, saying, "Son of a fatherless man, born of a harlot, how dare you insult us?
Jīvaka was taken aback; he remained silent and did not answer.
He returned home and asked his mother, saying,
"I looked at those sons of yours and saw that none were my equal, yet you instead reviled me, saying,
'You son of a fatherless man!'"
"Where is my father now? His mother replied,
"Your father is none other than King Bimbisāra."
Jīvaka said: "King Bimbisāra resides in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, five hundred li from here; by what cause could he have fathered me?
If it is as my mother says, how can this be proven?"
The mother then took out a seal-ring and showed it to him, saying, "This is your father’s ring.
Jīvaka examined it and saw the inscription of King Bimbisāra’s seal; he then took the ring and went to Rājagṛha.
He entered the palace gate directly; no one stopped him at the door, and he arrived before the king.
He paid his respects to the king, knelt for a long time, and said to him:

"I am a prince, born of Queen Nāḍī. This year I have reached the age of eight, and only now do I realize that I am of the Great King’s lineage. Therefore, carrying this ring as a token of my identity, I have come from afar to return home."
When the king saw the inscription on the seal, he recalled his former vow and realized that this was indeed his son; overcome with grief and compassion, he appointed him as the crown prince.
After two years had passed, King Ajātaśatru was born, whereupon Jīvaka addressed the king, saying:
"At the time of my birth, I held a pouch of needles and medicine in my hand; therefore, I am destined to be a physician."
"Although the King regards me as his crown prince, this is not what I desire.
Now that the King has fathered a legitimate son who shall succeed to the noble lineage, I wish to go forth and study the art of medicine."
The king then granted his request and said, "If you do not become the crown prince, you shall not eat the king's stipend in vain; you must study the way of medicine.

The king immediately issued a decree to all the foremost physicians in the kingdom, ordering them to teach him their entire art. However, Jīvaka merely engaged in play and never underwent formal training.
The various masters rebuked him, saying:
"This medical art is base and vulgar; it is truly not fit for the Most Honored Prince to study. Nevertheless, the Great King’s command must not be disobeyed or neglected."

"Since receiving Your Majesty's decree, many days and months have passed, yet the Crown Prince has not accepted even half a word of instruction. If the King were to question me, how could I possibly respond?"

Jīvaka said, "I was born with the certification of a physician in my hand; therefore, I informed the Great King that I would renounce my noble title to seek the study of medical arts. How could I possibly be indolent or require my teacher’s urging?"
"It is simply because the Way of our various masters is not worthy of being studied.

He then took up the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia), medical prescriptions, and various sutras on acupuncture and pulse diagnosis, posing detailed questions to the masters. The masters were driven to exhaustion and had no answers; they all bowed down and paid homage to Jīvaka, kneeling for a long time with palms joined, saying:
"Today we have come to know even more of the Prince’s divine sageliness; he truly is beyond our reach."

"The matters we have just asked about are all points of doubt that our teacher has been unable to resolve throughout his many lifetimes. We pray that the Prince will explain them in full detail, so as to untie the knots of ignorance within us since birth."

Jīvaka then explained the meaning of it for them; all the physicians were filled with joy and rose once more, prostrating themselves with their heads at his feet to pay homage, and they accepted his teaching.
At that time, Jīvaka thought to himself:
"The King has commanded all the physicians, yet there is nothing among them from whom I can learn. Who then shall teach me the way of medicine?"
At that time, I heard that in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā there was a physician of the Atreya clan named Bhela, who was exceptionally skilled in the medical arts and could teach me.
At that time, the youth Jīvaka went to that country, approached Piṅgala, and said:
"Great Master!
I now request you to be my preceptor."
Having studied the medical arts for seven years, he thought to himself:
"When will my training in the medical arts ever come to an end?
He then went to his teacher and said:
"I am now practicing the art of medicine; when will it ever come to an end?
At that time, the teacher immediately gave him a basket and tools for digging herbs, saying:
"You should go within a yojana around the city of Takṣaśilā and seek out various herbs; bring back any that are not medicinal."

Then Jīvaka, following his teacher’s instructions, searched for one *yojana* in every direction throughout the kingdom of Takṣaśilā for anything that was not medicinal. Having completed the circuit, he found nothing that was not medicinal; among all the plants, trees, and other objects he beheld, he was able to skillfully distinguish and know their respective uses, and there was nothing that was not a medicine.
He immediately returned empty-handed and went to his teacher’s place, saying these words:

"Master, you should know now that when I searched for non-medicinal plants throughout the entire circumference of one yojana in the kingdom of Takṣaśilā, I did not see anything that was not medicinal; every herb and tree I saw, I was able to distinguish, as well as its specific application."
The Master replied to Jīvaka, saying:
"You may go now; you have perfected the Way of Medicine.
Among all those in Jambudvīpa, you shall be the foremost."
"If I should die, you shall follow me next.
Thereupon, Jīvaka proceeded to treat illnesses, and every case he treated was healed; he thus became renowned throughout the kingdom.

Later, as he was about to enter the palace, he encountered a young boy carrying firewood before the palace gate; Jīvaka gazed at him and saw all the boy’s five viscera, intestines, and stomach with every detail clearly visible.
Jīvaka thought to himself:
"The *Bencao Jing* states that there is a 'King of Medicines' tree which, when viewed from the outside, illuminates the interior so that one can see the internal organs of a person.
Could this child have found such a King of Medicines among the firewood?"
He immediately went to ask the boy,
"How much do you want for the firewood?
The boy replied:
"Ten coins," he said,
and was hired for that sum to take the firewood.
Having unloaded the wood and placed it on the ground, it was so dark that he could not see the contents within.
Jīvaka further reflected in his mind:
"I do not know which among these bundles is the King of Medicines.
He then untied both bundles and took out each item one by one, placing them upon the child's abdomen; seeing no effect, he repeatedly took more out until both bundles of firewood were exhausted.
Finally, there remained a small branch about a foot long; he tried taking it to use as a mirror and could see clearly into his own abdomen.
Ji Yu was greatly delighted, realizing that this small branch must certainly be the "Medicine King," and he returned all the boy's firewood to him.
Once the boy had obtained the money, the woodcutter returned to his former state and departed with joy.
At that time, Jīvaka thought to himself:
"Whom should I treat first?"
"Since this country is small and located on the frontier,
it would be better for me now to return to my own land to begin opening up the path of medicine.
Thereupon, he returned to the city of Pāṭaliputra.
In the city of Vārāṇasī, there was a great elder whose wife suffered from chronic headaches for twelve years; though many physicians treated her, they were unable to cure her.
When Jīvaka heard this, he went immediately to the house and said to the gatekeeper,
"Inform the Elder that there is a physician standing outside the gate.
Thereupon, the gatekeeper entered and informed him.
“There is a physician outside the gate.
The householder’s wife asked,
“What does the physician look like?”
He replied, “It is a youth.
He then thought to himself:
"The elder physicians have treated me and yet I am not cured; how much less so, then, those who are young?
He then commanded his gatekeeper, saying, "I have no need for physicians now."
The gatekeeper immediately went out and said:
"I have already informed the elder on your behalf; the elder’s wife said:
'There is no need for a physician at this time.'"
Jīvaka spoke again:
"You may inform your householder’s wife that she should simply allow me to treat her; if she recovers, she may give me whatever she wishes."
Then the gatekeeper spoke to him again:
"The physician said this:
'Simply allow me to treat you; if you are cured, give me whatever you wish.'"
Having heard this, the householder’s wife thought to herself,
"If it is thus, there will be no harm.
She then commanded the gatekeeper to call him in.
At that time, Jīvaka entered the house of the elder’s wife and asked,
"What is troubling you?
She replied, "I am suffering from such-and-such."
He asked again,
"From what does the illness arise?
He replied, "It arises from such-and-such."
He asked again,
"How long has it been since you fell ill?
He replied, "I have been ill for such a length of time."
Having been questioned thus, he said, "I can cure you.
He then took excellent medicine and boiled it with ghee; he poured it into the elder’s wife's nose, and from the patient's mouth, both ghee and saliva came out together.
At that time, the patient immediately caught it in a vessel; he took the ghee but spat out and discarded the rest.
When Jīvaka saw this, his heart was filled with sorrow and distress, thinking:
"If he is so stingy as to begrudge even such a small amount of impure ghee, how could he ever repay my kindness?"
When the patient saw him, he asked Jīvaka,
"Are you distressed? He replied:
"It is indeed so.
He asked, "For what reason are you distressed?"
He replied, "I thought to myself:
'This small amount of ghee is impure, yet he still begrudges it; how then could he ever repay me?'"
"It is for this reason that I am sorrowful.
The householder’s wife replied, "The management of a household is no easy matter; what benefit would there be in abandoning it?"
"These can be used for lighting lamps; therefore, collect them.
You need only treat the illness—why worry about such things?
He then treated him, and subsequently the illness was cured.
At that time, the elder’s wife gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold, along with male and female slaves, carriages, and horses.
Having received these goods, Jīvaka returned to the city of Rājagṛha and went to the gate of Prince Abhaya, saying to the gatekeeper:
"Go and inform the prince, saying:"
“Jīvaka is outside.
The gatekeeper immediately went in and informed the king, who commanded the gatekeeper to call him in.
Once Jīvaka had entered, he prostrated himself before the king and stood to one side. He then related the preceding circumstances in detail to Prince Abhaya, saying:
"I shall offer all the goods I have obtained now to Your Majesty.
The prince said, "Stop; there is no need."
"Once you have made this offering, you may use it yourself.
This was Jīvaka’s first successful treatment of a disease.

At that time, in the kingdom of Kauśāmbī, there was the son of an elder who was playing on a wheel when his intestines became knotted within his abdomen; his food and drink could neither be digested nor pass out. There was no one in that country capable of treating him.
Hearing that there was a great physician in the kingdom of Magadha who was skilled at treating diseases, he immediately dispatched a messenger to inform the king:
"The son of the elder of Kauśāmbī is ill; Jīvaka is able to treat him. We pray that Your Majesty will send him here."
At that time, King Bimbisāra summoned Jīvaka and asked him, "The son of an elder in Kauśāmbī is ill; are you able to treat him?
He replied:
“Can you? “If you can, you may go and treat him.
Thereupon, Jīvaka mounted a carriage and went to Kauśāmbī.
When Jīvaka first arrived, the son of the elder had already died, and musicians were playing music as they escorted him out.
Hearing the sound, Jīvaka immediately asked,
"What kind of musical performance and drumming is this?"
A bystander replied, "The son of the elder for whom you came has already died; these are the sounds of his funeral music.
Jīvaka, being skilled in distinguishing all types of sound, immediately said:
"Make him turn back; this is not a dead man.
Having spoken these words, they immediately turned back.

At that time, Jīvaka descended from his carriage, took a sharp knife, and cut open the belly. He exposed the constricted place where the intestines were knotted and showed it to the parents and their relatives, saying:
"This is merely a plaything upon the wheel that has caused your intestines to become knotted in this manner; it prevents food and drink from being digested, yet it is not death.

He then released the abdomen, restored it to its original place, and sutured the skin and flesh together. He applied excellent medicinal ointment to it, whereupon the wound healed immediately, the hair grew back, and it was no different from a place that had never been wounded.

At that time, the elder’s son immediately repaid Jīvaka with four hundred thousand taels of gold; his wife also gave him four hundred thousand taels of gold, and the elder’s parents did likewise, each giving him four hundred thousand taels of gold.
Jīvaka thought to himself:
"As a teacher, one must repay their kindness.
I shall now take one million six hundred thousand taels of gold and give it to the great master Piṅgala of the country of Takṣaśilā."
Having thought thus, he took the gold and went to his teacher's place; prostrating with his head at the teacher's feet, he presented this gold, saying:
"I only pray that the Great Master will compassionately accept it!"
The Master said, "This already constitutes an offering; I have no need for this treasure.
Although Jīvaka was most earnest and persistent, Piṅgala accepted the gold. Jīvaka then took his leave, prostrated at his feet, and departed.
At that time, there was a daughter of a householder (gṛhapati) in the kingdom who was fifteen years old; on the very day she was about to be married, she suddenly died of a headache.
Jīvaka heard of this and went to her home, where he asked the girl’s father:
"What illness did this girl constantly suffer from that it led to her premature death?"

The father said, "Your daughter suffered from a slight headache, which has increased in severity over the days and months; this morning it flared up even more intensely than usual, leading to her passing away."

Jīvaka then stepped forward and used the King of Medicines to illuminate the interior of his head. He saw parasitic worms, large and small, reproducing one another in numbers reaching several hundred; they were boring into and eating his brain, and because the brain was exhausted, he had died. Jīvaka then used a golden blade to split open the head, extracted all the worms, and sealed them inside a jar.
He applied three kinds of divine ointments to the wound:
one was to mend the wound between the bones eaten by worms;
another was to produce brain matter.
One type of treatment was for external sword wounds.
He said to the girl’s father, “Ensure she remains calm and take care not to startle her; she shall recover in ten days and return to her former state. On that day, I shall come again.”
Just as Jīvaka had departed, the girl’s mother began to weep again, saying, "My son has died a second time!
How could anyone have torn open his head and brain only for him to return to life?"
"How can you, Father, bear to have someone seize your son in such a manner?
The father stopped him and said, "Jīvaka was born clutching a needle and medicine;
he has renounced noble rank and wealth to practice as a physician solely for the sake of all living beings. He is truly a King of Physicians ordained by Heaven—how could this be in vain?"
I entrusted you with these words, saying:
"Be careful not to cause him alarm.
Yet now you have done the opposite by weeping and crying, thereby startling him; this will surely cause the child to die and never be born again.
Upon hearing her father’s words, the mother ceased weeping and together with him cared for her; she remained in a state of tranquility for seven days.
At dawn on the seventh day, the girl exhaled deeply and awoke, as if rising from sleep, and said:
"I no longer have a headache at all; my body is entirely at ease."
"Who protected me so that I might become like this?

His father said, "You had already died previously; it was because the King of Physicians, Jīvaka, came to protect you, split open your head to extract the worm, and thereby enabled you to regain life."
He then opened the jar, took out the worms, and showed them to her. Upon seeing this, the woman was struck with great terror, yet she felt profound relief and congratulated herself, saying:
"Jīvaka’s divine power is truly such as this; I shall quickly repay his kindness."
The father said, "Jīvaka made an appointment with me, saying he would come today.
Then, in a brief moment, Jīvaka arrived. The girl joyfully went out the gate to meet him, prostrated herself with her head at his feet, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and said:
"I wish to become a maidservant to Jīvaka and serve you for the rest of my life to repay the kindness of my rebirth.
Jīvaka said, "I am a physician who travels everywhere to treat the sick; as I have no fixed dwelling, what use would I have for a maidservant?"
"If you truly wish to repay my kindness, give me five hundred taels of gold.

I have no need for this gold; the reason I ask for it is that when an ordinary person studies the Way, they ought to offer thanks to their teacher. Although my teacher had nothing to teach me, I was once his disciple. Now that I have obtained your gold, I shall give it to him."
The woman then presented five hundred taels of gold to Jīvaka.
Jīvaka accepted it and gave it to his teacher, then addressed the king:
"I shall return briefly to visit my mother and go to the kingdom of Vaiśālī."

At that time, there was also the son of a householder (*gṛhapati*) in the kingdom who was fond of martial arts; he fashioned a wooden horse over seven feet high and practiced riding it every day, beginning with his initial training.
Just as he had mounted his horse, after riding for some time and becoming increasingly practiced, he suddenly lost his balance and fell to the ground, dying.

When Ji Yu heard of this, he went at once and used the "Medicine King" to examine the interior of the belly; he saw that the liver was inverted and twisted toward the back, and because the vital qi was knotted and could not pass through, the man had died.

Furthermore, he used a golden knife to cut open his abdomen and reached in with his hand to arrange the organs; having returned the liver to its forward position, he applied three kinds of divine ointments:
one to heal the places where his hand had grasped and handled the organs, and another to facilitate the flow of the vital breaths.
A certain person was wounded by a blade;
before he died, he instructed his father, saying:
"Be careful not to let him be startled; he shall recover in three days."
The father, having received these instructions, tended to him with quiet care.
On the third day, the child exhaled and awoke; appearing as if rising from sleep, he immediately sat up.
In a short while, Jīvaka also arrived. The boy joyfully went out to meet him, prostrated himself at his feet in greeting, and knelt for a long time, saying:
"I wish to become Jīvaka’s slave and serve him for the rest of my life, in order to repay the kindness of being restored to life."
Jīvaka said, "I am a physician who travels everywhere to treat illnesses; the families of the sick vie with one another to employ me as their servant, so why would I need a slave?"
"My mother raised me with great toil and hardship, yet I have not yet repaid her for her kindness through offerings.
If you wish to express gratitude for my debt, you may give me five hundred taels of gold to repay my mother's kindness."
Thereupon, he took the gold and presented it to the daughter of Nanda, returning to the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
Jīvaka treated these four individuals, and his fame spread throughout the world; there was no one who did not hear of or know him.
Furthermore, to the south there was a great kingdom, eight thousand *li* from Rājagṛha, over which King Bimbisāra and all the minor kingdoms were subjects.

The king had been ill for many years without recovery; he was constantly tormented by anger and would kill people at the mere sight of them—he would kill someone if they looked up at him, and kill them even if they lowered their heads and did not look up; he would kill someone if they walked slowly, and kill them even if they ran fast.
The attendants on his left and right did not know where to place their hands or feet.
When physicians prepared medicines, they were immediately filled with suspicion that they might contain poison, and so they killed them as well.
The number of court officials, palace women, and physicians killed before and after could not be counted.
His illness grew increasingly severe; a toxic heat assailed his heart, leaving him agitated and short of breath, as if his body were being consumed by fire.
Upon hearing that Jīvaka was there, he immediately issued an edict commanding King Bimbisāra to summon Jīvaka.

When Jīvaka heard that this king had killed many physicians, he was greatly terrified. King Bimbisāra, moreover, pitied him for his youth and feared he might be killed; though he wished not to send him away, he feared being executed himself. Father and son remained together, sorrowful day and night, not knowing what plan to adopt.
At that time, King Bimbisāra took Jīvaka with him and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating himself at the Buddha’s feet, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
That king is of a wicked nature and may kill the physician; is it appropriate for us to go?”
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"In a previous life, you and I made a vow together that we would both protect and deliver the world; I shall treat internal illnesses, and you shall treat external illnesses."
"Now that I have attained Buddhahood, you have appeared before me in accordance with my original vow.
This king is critically ill and has come from afar to welcome you; why do you not go?
Go quickly to rescue and protect him, and act with skillful means so that his illness will surely be cured and the king will not kill you."

Jīvaka, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, went to the king’s presence. He examined the king’s pulse and used the King of Medicines to illuminate him; he saw that within the king’s five viscera and hundred vessels, the blood and qi were turbulent, entirely consisting of the venom of snakes and pythons pervading his entire body.
Jīvaka said to the king:
"The King’s illness can be cured; with treatment, recovery is assured. However, you must enter the presence of the Queen Mother to consult regarding the preparation of the medicine.
If you do not see the Queen Mother, the medicine will ultimately not be completed."

When the king heard these words, he did not understand their cause and felt a deep urge to be angry; however, as he suffered from his own illness and had previously heard of Jīvaka’s reputation, he went out to meet him from afar, hoping for certain benefit. Furthermore, thinking that the man was but a youth and could have no ulterior motives, he suppressed his anger and listened to him.
He immediately dispatched a eunuch in green robes to lead him in to see the Empress Dowager.
Zhi Yu addressed the Empress Dowager, saying:
"The King’s illness can be cured. I shall now prepare the medicine; you should secretly transmit the prescription and not disclose it to others. You ought to clear the attendants from our presence."
The Empress Dowager immediately dismissed the maidservants and eunuchs.
Zhiyu then addressed the Empress Dowager, saying:
"In examining the King's illness, I see that the blood and qi within his body are entirely the venom of snakes and pythons; he does not seem to be human."
"Who is the father of this king?
Tell me the truth, O Queen; if I can cure him, I shall do so, but if you do not tell me, the king's illness cannot be healed."

The Empress Dowager said, "In the past, while I was sleeping during the day in the Golden Pillar Hall, a being suddenly came and pressed down upon me. At that time, I was in a state between waking and dreaming, as if in a nightmare; I then entered into intimacy with it."
Suddenly I awoke and saw a great python, over three zhang in length, gliding past me; I felt as though it had a physical body.
The King was indeed the son of that python, yet out of shame I never spoke of it.
"Boy, you have now realized this; how marvelous and divine!
If the illness can be cured, I wish to entrust the royal command to you, boy.
To treat it now, what medicine should be used?"
Jīvaka replied,
“There is only ghee.
The Empress Dowager said:

"Alas! Young man, be careful not to speak of *amṛta*. The Great King detests the scent of *amṛta* and also detests the very name of *amṛta*; previously and subsequently, there have been several thousand people who died simply from speaking the word 'amṛta' while seated before him."
"If you speak these words now, they will surely kill you.
This drink will never go down when given to the King; I pray you, use another medicine instead. Jīvaka said:
"Clarified butter (sarpis) cures poison; it is precisely because those suffering from poisonous ailments detest hearing of clarified butter that [it is not used].
If the King’s illness were slight or were caused by other poisons, there would be other medicines capable of curing it."
Since the venom of the python is so potent and has already permeated his entire body, it could not possibly be neutralized except by *amṛta* (the supreme essence).
We shall now boil and refine it to transform it into water, rendered odorless and tasteless; the King will not perceive it, and he shall drink it of his own accord.
"The medicine will surely cure him once administered; there is no need for concern.
He then went out and saw the King, saying:
"I entered earlier and saw the Empress Dowager; I have already presented the prescription. It shall now be compounded, and it will be ready in fifteen days."
"Now I have five wishes; if the King grants them, my illness may be cured immediately, but if he does not grant them, my illness cannot be cured.
The King asked, "What are these five wishes?"
Jīvaka said: "First, I wish to obtain new clothes from the King's inner storehouse that have not yet been worn on a body;
second, I wish to be permitted to enter and exit alone, without being stopped at the gate."
"Third, I pray that I may enter alone every day to see the Empress Dowager and the Queen, and that no one forbid or scold me;
fourth, I pray that when the King drinks the medicine, he shall drink it all at once with a single draught and not pause midway;
fifth, I pray that I may obtain the King’s eight-thousand-li white elephant so that I may ride it."
Upon hearing this, the king was greatly incensed and said,
"How dare my son seek these five boons?
Explain them to me at once!"
"If you cannot explain this, I shall now beat you to death.
How dare you ask me for my new clothes?
Do you wish to kill me and then put on my garments to falsely impersonate my person?"

Jīvaka said, “In compounding medicine, one ought to be pure and observe the precepts of purification (*upavāsa*). However, I have been traveling for a long time, and my robes are covered in dust and grime; therefore, I wish to obtain the King’s robes in order to compound the medicine.”
The king’s mind was relieved, and he said:
"This is most excellent!
Why do you wish to enter and exit the palace gates yourself without being subject to restrictions or reprimands?"
"Do you intend to lead troops here to attack and kill me?

Jīvaka replied, "Your Majesty has previously employed various physicians, yet you have harbored suspicions toward them all, never entrusting them with full confidence; furthermore, you have executed them and refused to take their medicine."

The ministers all said, "The King would surely have had us killed again; however, the King’s illness is now extremely severe, and we fear that outsiders may harbor rebellious intentions and cause a disturbance.

If you allow us to enter and exit at our own discretion without being forbidden or rebuked, then everyone, both great and small, will know that the King trusts us. They will certainly take our medicine, and his illness will surely be cured; thus, they will not dare to harbor thoughts of rebellion."
The king said, "Excellent!
Why do you enter alone every day to see my mother and my wife?"
"Do you wish to commit lewd disorder?
Jīvaka replied, "The King has killed many people before and after;
the ministers, both high and low, each harbor fear and none wish for the King's well-being. There is no one who can be trusted."
"Now we are mixing medicine together; if he were to administer poison while I am momentarily distracted by my glance, I would not even notice it—this is no small matter.
Therefore, I reflect that those who are trustworthy and whose affection is undivided are only one's mother and wife."
Therefore, I venture to enter and see the Empress Dowager and the Queen to prepare the medicine with them.
Since it takes fifteen days of decoction before it is completed, I wish to enter every day to monitor the consistency of the fire.
The king said, "Excellent!
Why did you cause me to drink this medicine in a single draught until it was finished, not allowing me to stop midway?"
"Is it because you wish to poison me internally, fearing that I might perceive it?
Jīvaka replied, "Medicines have their prescribed proportions;
their potency and flavor ought to reach one another. If there were a lapse in the middle, the potency would not be continuous."
The king said, "Excellent!
Why do you wish to have my elephant to ride?"

"This elephant is the national treasure of our country; it travels eight thousand li in a single day. It is precisely by relying on this elephant that we have intimidated and subdued all other nations.
Do you wish to ride it because you intend to steal it back to your home to join forces with your father and attack our country?"

Jīvaka said, "In the mountains of the southern border there is a divine and wondrous medicinal herb, four thousand li from here. Your Majesty should drink the medicine now so that you may obtain this herb immediately; you must take it again once obtained, and for this purpose I wish to ride this elephant to go and gather it, departing in the morning and returning by evening, so that the potency of the medicine remains intact."
The king’s mind was greatly relieved, and he granted them all permission.

Thereupon, Jīvaka refined the *sarpirmaṇḍa* (clarified butter essence); it was completed on the fifteenth day, transformed into something like clear water. Having obtained five *śuṅgā* (measures) in total, he presented it to the Empress Dowager and the Queen; together they carried the medicine out and addressed the king, saying, "Please take this."
"I pray that you will have a white elephant stationed before the palace in advance.
The king immediately granted his consent.

When the king saw the medicine, it appeared only as clear water; it had no scent or flavor whatsoever, and he did not recognize it as *amṛta* (clarified butter). Furthermore, the Empress Dowager and the Queen personally supervised its preparation, and believing it was not poison, he fulfilled their original request by drinking it all at once.
Jīvaka then mounted an elephant and set out directly for the kingdom of Rājagṛha.

At that time, Jīvaka had traveled exactly three thousand li; as he was young and his physical strength was still slight, he could not endure the rapid pace. His head spun and he was utterly exhausted, so he stopped to rest and lie down.
When midday had passed, the king let out a belch and smelled the stench of *sarpis* (clarified butter).
He became even more enraged and said, "This child dares to poison me with *sarpis*! It is no wonder he sought my white elephant; he truly intends to rebel and flee."
The king had a heroic minister named Wu, whose supernatural power of foot-speed could match that of this elephant. He immediately called out to Wu, saying:
"Go quickly to pursue and seize the boy; bring him back alive, for I wish to have him beaten to death before my very eyes."
"By nature you have always been lacking in integrity and greedy for food; therefore, you are called a 'crow' (kāka).
These physicians are often fond of administering poison; if your son prepares food for you, be careful not to eat it!"
Having received the command, the crow went forth and caught up with him in the mountains, saying:
"For what reason do you take the King of All Medicines from the *sarpis* (clarified butter) and claim it to be medicine?"
"The King has therefore sent me to summon you back; you must follow me home at once. If you offer your apologies and confess, there is perhaps hope for your life;
if you persist in fleeing, you shall certainly be killed now and never escape."
Jīvaka thought to himself:
"Although I have employed skillful means to seek this white elephant, I still cannot escape; I must now employ further skillful means—how can I simply go along with him?"
He then said to the crow, "I have not eaten since this morning; I shall surely die upon my return.
Would it not be better for you to grant me a brief moment so that I may eat fruit and drink water in the mountains, and then go to my death with a full stomach?"
When Eḷeyya saw the young boy Jīvaka, who was terrified of death and spoke with great distress, he felt pity for him and listened to him, saying:
"Eat quickly and we must depart; we cannot stay long."
Jīvaka then took a pear, ate half of it, and placed poison under his fingernails to smear onto the remaining half, which he set on the ground;
he then took a cup of water, drank half of it, and likewise applied the poison from beneath his nails to the remainder of the water, which he also set on the ground.
He then sighed and said:
"This water and these pears are both celestial medicines; they are both fragrant and delicious.
Those who consume them will find their bodies at peace, all their ailments will be cured, and their physical strength will double."
"It is a pity that he is not in the capital city so that the common people might all have access to him; instead, he is in the deep mountains where no one knows of his existence.
Having said this, he entered the mountains to search for him.

The nature of crows is greedy; they cannot restrain themselves regarding food and drink. Furthermore, having heard Jīvaka praise it as a divine medicine and seeing that Jīvaka himself had already consumed it, they concluded there was certainly no poison. They then took the remaining pears to eat and drank all the remaining water.

He immediately suffered from diarrhea, with the discharge flowing like a torrent of water; he collapsed to the ground and lay there, falling into a dizzy spell whenever he attempted to rise, unable to move again.

Jīvyarāja said, "If Your Majesty takes my medicine, the illness will surely be cured. However, the power of the medicine has not yet taken effect and the remaining toxins have not been exhausted; if I were to go now, you would certainly kill me."

"You know nothing; you have risen with the desire to catch me so as to relieve the burden upon your body, and for that reason you have fallen ill. This illness is naturally without suffering, so be careful not to move; you shall recover in three days.
If you rise to pursue me, you will surely die, without a doubt."
He then mounted the elephant and departed.
Jīvaka passed through a village settlement and said to the headman:

"This is the king’s messenger; he has suddenly fallen ill. You must go quickly, carry him home, and tend to him well. Provide him with fine bedding and give him rice gruel; take care not to let him die, for if he dies, the King will destroy your kingdom."
Having finished speaking, he departed and returned to his own country.
Changwu received the imperial decree and went to welcome and care for him; after three days, the poison subsided and his bowels were cleared, whereupon the crow returned home.
Seeing the King, he prostrated himself with his head at the ground and spoke of his own accord:

"I am truly foolish and have violated Your Majesty’s instructions. Believing the words of Jīvaka, I ate the remains of his fruit and was struck by it; I suffered from diarrhea for three days, and though I have only just recovered this morning, I know that I am destined to die."
Within three days of the crow's return, the king’s illness had already been cured.
The king reflected to himself, "I regret having sent the crow away.
Seeing the crow return, he said, feeling both sorrow and joy:
"If you had not brought the child here immediately, I would have surely beaten him to death when I was in my rage.
I owe him a debt of gratitude for saving my life; that you, on the contrary, should kill him is a grave act of perversity."
He immediately repented for all those he had previously wronged by killing, providing them with lavish funerals once more, restoring their families, and bestowing wealth upon them.
Longing to see Jīvaka and wishing to repay his kindness, he dispatched a messenger to welcome Jīvaka back.
Although Jīvaka knew that the King’s illness had already been cured, he still harbored lingering fear and did not wish to go again.
At that time, Jīvaka went once more to the Buddha’s dwelling, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"The king has sent a messenger to summon you; should you go?
The Buddha told Jīvaka, "In your past lives, you already made a great vow that you would accomplish meritorious virtue; how can you stop midway?"
"Now you must go once more; you have already treated his external illness, and I too shall treat his internal illness.
Jīvaka then followed the messenger and departed. When the king saw Jīvaka, he was greatly delighted; he invited him to sit with him and, taking hold of his arm, said:
"I rely upon the grace of your benevolence to have been restored to life once more. How shall I repay you?"

"I shall divide the kingdom and give half to you; the palace ladies, as well as the treasures and stores within the treasury, shall all be divided in half. I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will accept them."
Jīvaka said, “I was originally a crown prince;
although it was indeed a small kingdom, it had its own subjects and was fully endowed with precious treasures.
Because I did not delight in governing a kingdom, I sought to become a physician. Since I shall practice the healing of diseases, what use would I have for land, court ladies, or precious objects?”
"None of these are what I require.
Previously, Your Majesty granted me five wishes, and my external illness has already been cured; now, if you would grant one wish, my internal illness may likewise be healed."
The king said, "I shall surely follow your benevolent instruction; I request to hear further concerning one of your wishes.
Jīvaka replied:
"I pray that Your Majesty will invite the Buddha and receive the Dharma from him," [he said],
because the King had spoken of the Buddha’s merits as being sublime and uniquely venerable.
Upon hearing this, the King was greatly delighted and said:
"Now I wish to dispatch Ucchṅga to welcome the Buddha with a white elephant; can he be brought here?
Jīvaka replied, "There is no need for a white elephant;
the Buddha understands all things and knows the thoughts in people's minds from afar."

"Simply observe the fast and maintain purity, prepare the offerings and burn incense, and prostrate toward the Buddha from afar. As you kneel long and offer your formal invitation, the Buddha will surely come in person.
The king acted according to these words.
The next day, the Buddha arrived together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. When the meal was finished, he preached the sutra for the king.

The king’s mind was opened and enlightened, and he immediately gave rise to the aspiration for supreme, perfect, and true enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*). All those in the kingdom, both great and small, received the five precepts; they paid their respects with reverence and departed.

Furthermore, since Nandā’s birth was extraordinary, she was also exceptionally intelligent as she grew up. She studied under her father and became widely learned in the scriptures, the Way, astrology, and various arts; she surpassed her father in these matters and, moreover, attained mastery in vocal music, her voice being like that of Brahmā.
Five hundred women from the families of various *gṛhapatis* and brahmins all went to follow her studies, regarding her as their great teacher.
The woman Āmrapālī constantly led five hundred disciples, instructing them in the arts and scriptures; at times they would play together in gardens and ponds or perform music.
The people of the country did not understand the reason for this and began to slander her, calling her a "prostitute," while her five hundred disciples were all labeled as a "prostitute's faction.
Furthermore, when Nanda was born, there were also two other girls in the country named Sumana and Puṇḍarīkā, who were born at the same time.

As for the *sumana* maiden, she was born from within a *sumana* flower. In a country there was a householder’s family who constantly pressed *sumana* flowers to make fragrant oil. Beside the stone used for pressing the oil, a tumor-like node suddenly formed, as large as a pellet ball; it grew larger day by day until it was the size of a fist. The stone then burst open, and from within the node of the stone, a cluster appeared. This cluster was like fireflies, shooting out and falling to the ground. After three days, a *sumana* sprouted, and after another three days, it became a flower. From within that flower, the maiden was born. Because she was born from a *sumana* flower, she was named *Sumana*. She grew up and eventually married a man of the same clan. Later, she gave birth to a son. When the son reached the age of seven, he asked his mother, "Where did I come from before being born here? His mother replied, "I do not know. The son said, "If you do not know, I shall go and ask my father. He went to his father and asked, "Father, where did I come from before being born here? His father replied, "I do not know either. The son said, "If you both do not know, I shall go and ask Grandfather. He went to his grandfather and asked, "Grandfather, where did I come from before being born here? His grandfather replied, "I do not know. The son said, "If you do not know, I shall go and ask Great-Grandfather. He went to Great-Grandfather and asked, "Great-Grandfather, where did I come from before being born here? Great-Grandfather replied, "I do not know. The son said, "If you do not know, I shall go and ask Great-Great-Grandfather. He went to Great-Great-Grandfather and asked, "Great-Great-Grandfather, where did I come from before being born here? Great-Great-Grandfather replied, "I do not know. The son said, "If you do not know, I shall go and ask Great-Great-Great-Grandfather. He went to Great-Great-Great-Grandfather and asked, "Great-Great-Great-Grandfather, where did I come from before being born here? Great-Great-Great-Grandfather replied, "I do not know. Within the blooming flower was a young girl; the householder took her in and raised her, naming her Sumanā. As she grew up, she was exceptionally beautiful, and her talent, brilliance, and wisdom were second only to those of Ambapālī.

At that time, moreover, in the bathing pool of a brahmin’s household, blue lotuses grew spontaneously; these flowers were exceptionally large and increased in size day by day until they resembled five-sheng jars.

When the flower opened, she saw a girl within it; the Brahmin took her and raised her, naming her Pāṭhā. As she grew up, she was beautiful and possessed of talent, brilliance, and wisdom equal to that of Sumanā.
When the various kings heard that these two maidens possessed a beauty unsurpassed in the world, they all came to seek them in marriage.

The two maidens said, "Our birth did not proceed from a womb, but rather we emerged from within a flower in the grass; thus we are different from ordinary people. Why should we follow the ways of worldly men and marry again?"

Hearing that the maiden Nanda was intelligent and her beauty was peerless in the world, with no one to equal her, and furthermore that she had been born as his own sister, they all took leave of their parents to serve Nanda and seek to become her disciples; in their mastery of the scriptures and wisdom, they all surpassed these five hundred men.

At that time, the Buddha entered the kingdom of Vaiśālī. The Mango Girl (Amrapālī) then led five hundred of her disciples out to welcome the Buddha; she prostrated herself with her head at his feet and, kneeling for a long time, addressed him, saying:
"I pray that the Buddha will come to my garden tomorrow to partake of a meal."
The Buddha accepted her invitation by remaining silent.
The daughter of the Āmra tree returned home and prepared the offerings.
As the Buddha entered the city, the king again came out from his palace to welcome him; having completed his prostrations, he knelt for a long time and entreated the Buddha:
"I pray that you will come to the palace tomorrow for a meal.
The Buddha said, "The maiden Nanda has already invited me previously; the King shall go later."
The King said:
"I am the king, and I have invited the Buddha with the utmost sincerity; I certainly hope for his acceptance.
This Nanda woman is merely a courtesan who daily leads five hundred female disciples of her own to engage in unrighteous conduct. Why would he abandon me to accept her invitation?"
The Buddha said, "This woman is not a courtesan; she possesses great merit from her past lives and has already made offerings to three hundred million Buddhas.

In the past, she was once a sister along with the women Sumanā and Pāṭalā. Of them, Nāḍī was the eldest, Sumanā was next, and Pāṭalā was the youngest. They were born into a family of great lineage, possessing abundant wealth and treasures. The sisters led one another in making offerings to five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, providing them daily with food and drink as well as clothing, supplying whatever they lacked until the end of their lives."
The three of them constantly made this vow:
"May we, in future lives, encounter a Buddha and attain spontaneous transformation-birth, not through a womb, remaining far removed from defilement and impurity."
"Now, in accordance with her original vow, she has been born to meet me at this time.

Furthermore, although she formerly made offerings to bhikṣuṇīs, she was the daughter of a wealthy family; her speech was coquettish and overflowing, and from time to time she would mock the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:

'You practitioners have lived in this town for a long time; you must surely wish to marry. It is only because we provide for you and keep you in check that you cannot indulge your feelings as you please.'"
Therefore, I now undergo these remaining karmic retributions; though I daily praise the Way of the Sūtras, I am falsely slandered for my licentiousness.

These five hundred disciples also exerted their strength together at that time to assist me in making offerings with a single-minded joy; thus they have been born together in this life, and as a result, they continue to follow one another.

"At that time, Jīvaka was the son of a poor family. Seeing the Nanda maiden making offerings, his heart was filled with deep admiration and joy; yet, lacking the means, he would constantly sweep for the bhikṣuṇīs. Having finished sweeping them clean, he would immediately make this vow:
'May I be able to sweep away the bodily diseases and impurities of all people in the world as thoroughly as this! "
"The daughter of the Nāla clan took pity on his poverty and, seeing his diligent efforts, constantly addressed him as her son.
Whenever that bhikṣuṇī was ill, she would always have Jīvaka summon a physician and prepare decoctions, saying:
'May you, in future lives, together with me, obtain this merit.'"
Jīvaka treated all those he encountered with medicine, and they were completely healed. He then made a vow, saying:
"May I, in future lives, become a Great King of Physicians, constantly treating the diseases of the four great elements of all bodies, so that wherever I go, all may be cured."
"All this is due to causes and conditions from former days; it is for this reason that they have now become the children of the Nāla girl, all in accordance with their original vows.
When the king heard the Buddha’s words, he knelt down for a long time to repent his transgressions and postponed [the marriage] until a later day.
The next day, the Buddha went with the bhikṣus to the mango grove of the three daughters and fully explained for them the merit of their original vows.

Upon hearing the sutra, the three daughters attained understanding; together with their five hundred disciples, they simultaneously rejoiced in leaving the household life to practice the path. Through diligent and unremitting effort, they all attained the state of Arhatship.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“You should receive and uphold this, and explain it for the fourfold assembly so that it does not come to an end.
All sentient beings must be careful with their body, speech, and mind, and must not give rise to arrogance or negligence.”
In the past, because the woman Nanda mocked and ridiculed a bhikṣuṇī, she has now been falsely accused of sexual misconduct.
You should cultivate the actions of body, speech, and mind, and constantly make virtuous vows; those who hear this should rejoice, believe with gladness, and uphold it.

Do not give rise to slander, lest you fall into hell; as a residual retribution, you will be born as an animal for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Thereafter, as a human retribution, you will be poor and lowly, unable to hear the True Dharma, born into a family of false views, constantly encountering evil kings, and physically incomplete.
"You should practice, uphold, read, and recite it, ensuring that it never ceases throughout the limits of the future.
At that time, Ānanda rose from his seat, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with palms joined, and addressed the Buddha,
saying, "World-Honored One!"
"What should this essential teaching be called? The Buddha said to Ānanda:

"This sutra is titled 'The Sutra on the Causes and Conditions of the Maiden Nāḍī and Jīvaka. The methods for its practice are as described above; one should make offerings to bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs, provide medicine and welcome physicians, rejoice in others' merit, and make vows. By doing so, one now obtains this fruit of retribution; thus should it be upheld."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the great assembly, the people, and the eight classes of beings—gods, dragons, and so forth—hearing what the Buddha had taught, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Thus ends the *Sutra Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions of the Woman Nāḍika and Jīvaka*.
